ibd-ca2198e848a9d5c8-q3:b.hint: Work is connected to the change in volume. On a pressure–volume graph, look for the relevant area.
notes: Work done by a gas is W = ∫p dV; at constant pressure it becomes pΔV. Expansion gives positive work by the gas, compression negative.
The enclosed area of a complete cycle is net work, with its sign set by the direction around the cycle. Convert kPa, MPa, litres and any axis multipliers before calculating.

ibd-ca2198e848a9d5c8-q3:c.hint: Draw the energy entering from the hot reservoir, the useful work and the energy rejected to the cold reservoir.
notes: Over a complete engine cycle ΔU = 0, so W = Q_hot − Q_cold and efficiency = W/Q_hot. Use energy per cycle or power consistently.
Only an ideal reversible Carnot engine reaches η = 1 − T_cold/T_hot. Both reservoir temperatures must be in kelvin; this gives an upper bound for a real engine.

duplicate-e93fb6aad223a11e.hint: Link the macroscopic quantity to the random motion and wall collisions of the molecules.
notes: Mean translational kinetic energy is 3kT/2 per molecule. The rms speed obeys v_rms = √(3kT/m), so molecular mass matters when comparing gases.
Pressure comes from the rate of momentum transfer to container walls. In the ideal model, particles have negligible volume and negligible interactions except during elastic collisions.

duplicate-bc4d8239cbc6a422.hint: Think about both the rate of wall collisions and the momentum change in each collision.
notes: Gas pressure is momentum transferred to the walls per unit time per unit area. Higher temperature increases typical molecular speeds and momentum transfer.
A smaller volume also increases collision frequency with the walls. Collisions between molecules alone are not the direct force exerted on a wall.
